questions.passage: Last spring, Maya organized a campus supply drive for local schools. Her older [brother, a chemistry major at the state university] helped her sort boxes of notebooks and calculators. Though the project began as a small class assignment, it soon grew into a community event. By June, more than two hundred families had received materials.
questions.q: Which choice is best for the bracketed portion?
options: brother, a chemistry major at the state university,
brother; a chemistry major at the state university;
brother: a chemistry major at the state university,
brother a chemistry major at the state university
questions.explanation: The phrase 'a chemistry major at the state university' is a nonessential appositive describing the brother, so commas are needed on both sides of it. A semicolon or colon would incorrectly separate the subject from its verb.

questions.topic: Usage: agreement, verb forms and pronouns
questions.passage: Each year, Westfield High School holds a science fair in the gymnasium. Students design experiments, build models, and explain their findings to volunteer judges. This year, the science department added a new category for environmental engineering. Each of the students [have submitted] a proposal describing how the project addresses a real-world problem. The judges will announce the winners on Friday.
questions.q: Which choice is best for the bracketed portion?
options: has submitted
were submitting
submit
have submitted
questions.explanation: The subject is 'Each,' which is singular, so it takes the singular verb 'has submitted.' The plural word 'students' is part of a prepositional phrase and does not control the verb.

questions.passage: At Lincoln Middle School, the garden club meets twice a week after classes. Members plant vegetables in raised beds behind the cafeteria. Some students water the plants before school, while others check for insects during lunch. [They also record the number of tomatoes and peppers each week.] This record helps the science club compare growth under different soil mixes. At the end of the season, the garden club donates extra produce to a local food pantry.
questions.q: The writer is considering deleting the bracketed sentence. Should the writer keep or delete that sentence?
options: Deleted, because it shifts the paragraph from gardening to cafeteria menus.
Deleted, because it repeats the information about watering the plants.
Kept, because it explains what record the following sentence refers to.
Kept, because it explains why extra produce is donated to a food pantry.
questions.explanation: The next sentence begins 'This record,' so the bracketed sentence is needed to identify what record is being discussed. Deleting it would leave the referent unclear; the sentence also fits the paragraph's focus on the garden club's work.

questions.passage: After weeks of designing, building, and testing, the robotics team finally completed its prototype for the regional competition. The team [finished the prototype, therefore they] tested it under competition conditions. To their surprise, the robot completed the obstacle course in under two minutes. The team now plans to improve the robot's grip before the final event.
questions.q: Which choice is best for the bracketed portion?
options: finished the prototype; therefore; they
finished the prototype therefore, they
finished the prototype; therefore, they
finished the prototype, therefore, they
questions.explanation: Two independent clauses are joined, so a semicolon is needed before 'therefore'; the conjunctive adverb also requires a comma after it. A comma before 'therefore' creates a comma splice, and a semicolon after 'therefore' incorrectly separates the adverb from its clause.

questions.topic: Usage: agreement, verb forms and pronouns
questions.passage: When the student council needed a new mural for the cafeteria, the art teacher asked Priya and [I] to sketch several ideas. Priya focused on geometric patterns, while I drew scenes from the school's history. The council selected elements from both sketches for the final design. The completed mural now covers the east wall near the main entrance.
questions.q: Which choice is best for the bracketed portion?
options: myself
me
mine
I
questions.explanation: The pronoun is the object of the verb 'asked,' so the objective form 'me' is required. 'I' is a subject pronoun, while 'myself' is reflexive and has no matching reflexive antecedent in this construction.

questions.topic: Usage: agreement, verb forms and pronouns
questions.passage: Last month, the city library surveyed students about weekend hours. Many students said they would use the library on Saturday mornings if it opened earlier. If the library [would have opened] at nine instead of noon, more students could have attended study sessions, according to the survey. The library board will discuss the results at its next meeting.
questions.q: Which choice is best for the bracketed portion?
options: opened
had opened
has opened
would have opened
questions.explanation: This is a past unreal conditional: the if-clause needs the past perfect 'had opened,' and the result clause correctly uses 'could have attended.' 'Would have opened' is a common error in an if-clause, and the other forms do not match the unreal past meaning.

questions.passage: Chef Elena Ruiz grew up in Tucson, where her grandmother taught her to make tamales. When she opened her restaurant, she wanted the menu to reflect both her family's traditions and the produce available nearby. [She replaces some of the corn masa with locally ground blue corn and adds roasted poblano peppers from a farm outside town.] Customers often say the dish tastes familiar yet new. Ruiz plans to add another family recipe to the menu next season.
questions.q: Which choice best accomplishes the writer's goal of explaining how Chef Ruiz adapts a traditional recipe to local ingredients?
options: Her grandmother's recipe card is written in Spanish and English.
She replaces some of the corn masa with locally ground blue corn and adds roasted poblano peppers from a farm outside town.
Tamales are traditionally wrapped in corn husks before they are steamed.
She has worked in several restaurants in Tucson and Phoenix.
questions.explanation: The sentence identifies specific substitutions and additions, showing how Chef Ruiz changes a traditional tamale recipe with local ingredients. The other choices give background about her career, the general tamale-making process, or a family artifact but do not explain her adaptation.

questions.passage: The first year of the community garden was a success. The plots produced hundreds of pounds of vegetables, and volunteers donated the extra produce to a food pantry. [Therefore], the garden still lacks a reliable water source, so the organizers are applying for a grant. If the grant is approved, the garden will install a drip irrigation system before next summer.
questions.q: Which choice is best for the bracketed portion?
options: For example
Therefore
However
Likewise
questions.explanation: The first part of the paragraph presents successes, while the next clause introduces a remaining problem, so a contrast transition is needed. 'However' marks that contrast; 'Therefore,' 'Likewise,' and 'For example' signal relationships that do not fit.

questions.passage: For the science fair, Ms. Okafor's students built models to demonstrate the water cycle. To assemble one model, students needed [three items a thermometer, a beaker, and a notebook] for recording observations. The model showed how water evaporates, condenses, and returns to the ground as precipitation. Visitors voted for their favorite display at the end of the day.
questions.q: Which choice is best for the bracketed portion?
options: three items, a thermometer, a beaker, and a notebook
three items; a thermometer, a beaker, and a notebook
three items: a thermometer, a beaker, and a notebook
three items a thermometer, a beaker, and a notebook
questions.explanation: The clause 'students needed three items' is complete, and the following series explains what the items are, so a colon is appropriate. A comma or missing punctuation blurs the list, and a semicolon should join independent clauses rather than introduce this series.

questions.passage: At Roosevelt High School, a student-run bike repair shop has become a popular after-school program. [Students learn to fix brakes, replace tires, and adjust gears under the supervision of a local mechanic.] The shop also gives repaired bicycles to students who need reliable transportation. Last year, the program restored thirty bicycles and kept dozens of old frames out of landfills.
questions.q: Which choice best accomplishes the writer's goal of emphasizing the practical skills students learn in the bike repair program?
options: Students learn to fix brakes, replace tires, and adjust gears under the supervision of a local mechanic.
Local mechanics often donate used parts to the shop.
Many students ride their bicycles to school every day.
The shop is located in a converted storage room near the gym.
questions.explanation: The sentence listing brake repair, tire replacement, and gear adjustment directly names practical skills students learn in the program. The other choices provide context about donated parts, the shop's location, or students' commuting habits but do not focus on skills taught.

questions.topic: Usage: agreement, verb forms and pronouns
questions.passage: At the neighborhood health fair, a stack of pamphlets about nutrition [were left] on the table near the entrance. Volunteers encouraged visitors to take one and to ask questions about the free cooking classes offered each week. The event, held in the school gym, drew families from across the neighborhood.
questions.q: Which choice best replaces the bracketed portion?
options: NO CHANGE
have been left
are leaving
was left
questions.explanation: The subject is the singular noun stack, not the plural noun pamphlets, so the singular verb was is required. The original wording, represented by NO CHANGE, uses a plural verb and does not agree; have been left and are leaving also fail to match the singular subject.

questions.passage: Before the robotics competition began, Ms. Alvarez reminded her students [to check; their batteries, their tools, and their safety goggles]. The team had spent months preparing, and no one wanted a loose wire to cause a problem. They had tested every connection twice, but a final inspection was still required.
questions.q: Which choice best replaces the bracketed portion?
options: to check their batteries, their tools; and their safety goggles
to check their batteries, their tools, and their safety goggles
NO CHANGE
to check their batteries; their tools, and their safety goggles
questions.explanation: A semicolon cannot separate the verb check from its direct objects, so no semicolon belongs after check. The items in the list should be separated by commas, and the semicolon placements in the other choices disrupt the list.

questions.passage: Many students at Riverside High School take part in the annual creek cleanup. [They collect trash along the bank they record what they find]. The data helps local scientists track pollution levels. Last year, more than sixty volunteers filled four large bags with plastic bottles and other debris.
questions.q: Which choice best replaces the bracketed portion?
options: They collect trash along the bank; and record what they find
They collect trash along the bank and record what they find
They collect trash along the bank, they record what they find
NO CHANGE
questions.explanation: The two actions share the subject They and can be joined with and in one complete sentence; no punctuation is needed before and in this compound predicate. A comma between the clauses would create a comma splice, and a semicolon before and leaves a fragment without an independent subject.

questions.topic: Knowledge of language: word choice, style and tone
questions.passage: The city council meeting grew tense as residents discussed the proposed bike lane. Some speakers worried about parking, while others pointed to safety. The council chair listened carefully and [told everyone that every concern would get looked into] before a vote was scheduled.
questions.q: Which choice best replaces the bracketed portion to maintain a formal, professional tone?
options: assured residents that every concern would be reviewed
NO CHANGE
let people know every concern would get looked into
told folks that every concern would be checked out
questions.explanation: The phrasing told everyone that every concern would get looked into is conversational and therefore does not suit a formal, professional tone. Assured residents that every concern would be reviewed is precise, formal, and appropriate for the council chair; the other choices use informal words such as folks, checked out, or get looked into.

questions.passage: The school's new greenhouse [which was funded by a grant from a local foundation] will open next month. Students will use it to grow herbs for the cafeteria and to study plant genetics. A ribbon-cutting ceremony is planned for the first day of spring.
questions.q: Which choice best replaces the bracketed portion?
options: , which was funded by a grant from a local foundation,
which was funded by a grant from a local foundation,
, which was funded by a grant from a local foundation
NO CHANGE
questions.explanation: The clause which was funded by a grant from a local foundation is nonessential information about the greenhouse, so it must be set off by commas on both sides. Without the comma before the clause, after it, or both, the sentence is incorrectly punctuated.

questions.passage: After reviewing the lab results, [the experiment was repeated by Dr. Chen because the first sample had been contaminated]. The second trial produced a clearer set of measurements. The class compared both sets of data during the next laboratory period.
questions.q: Which choice best replaces the bracketed portion?
options: NO CHANGE
because the first sample had been contaminated, the experiment was repeated by Dr. Chen
Dr. Chen repeated the experiment because the first sample had been contaminated
the experiment, because the first sample had been contaminated, was repeated by Dr. Chen
questions.explanation: The introductory phrase After reviewing the lab results must describe the subject of the main clause. Only Dr. Chen repeated the experiment makes Dr. Chen the one doing the reviewing; the choices beginning with the experiment leave the phrase dangling.

questions.topic: Knowledge of language: word choice, style and tone
questions.passage: During the student council debate, Priya argued that the school should replace its aging water fountains. Some classmates complained about the cost, but Priya [insisted that safe drinking water was a priority that could not be ignored]. Her calm but firm response convinced several students to support the proposal.
questions.q: Which choice best replaces the bracketed portion to make Priya's statement sound reasonable rather than overly dramatic?
options: demanded that the school stop wasting money on anything else until the fountains were fixed
declared that ignoring safe drinking water would be an absolute disgrace
NO CHANGE
noted that safe drinking water should remain a priority
questions.explanation: Noted that safe drinking water should remain a priority presents Priya's point in a calm, reasonable way. Insisted that safe drinking water was a priority that could not be ignored, declared that ignoring it would be an absolute disgrace, and demanded that the school stop wasting money are more forceful and dramatic.

questions.topic: Usage: agreement, verb forms and pronouns
questions.passage: The environmental science teacher recommended that each group [submits] a brief proposal before beginning its experiment. The proposal should explain the group's question, method, and expected timeline. Students will present their proposals to the class on Friday, and approved projects will receive a small budget for supplies.
questions.q: Which choice best replaces the bracketed portion?
options: NO CHANGE
submit
submitted
will submit
questions.explanation: After recommended that, American English uses the subjunctive mood, which takes the base form submit regardless of the singular phrase each group. Submits uses the ordinary singular present form, while submitted and will submit do not fit the subjunctive construction.

questions.topic: Knowledge of language: word choice, style and tone
questions.passage: Last spring, the Meadowbrook High School garden club started a seed library in the school library. Visitors can take seeds for free and leave seeds from their own gardens for others. [The club also meets on Thursdays after school in Room 214.] By sharing seeds, students and families can grow a wider variety of vegetables without spending much money.
questions.q: The writer wants to explain how the seed library works. Should the writer keep or delete the bracketed sentence?
options: Delete it, because it repeats information stated earlier in the paragraph.
Keep it, because it gives readers useful information about the club's schedule.
Delete it, because it does not explain how the seed library works.
Keep it, because it clarifies where the seed library is located.
questions.explanation: The paragraph explains how the seed library works: visitors take and leave seeds, and the community benefits. The club's meeting time in Room 214 is unrelated to that explanation, so deleting the sentence keeps the paragraph focused; it does not repeat earlier information.

questions.passage: Last year, the Westside Community Library opened a new reading room for students. The room has soft chairs, bright lamps, and a strict quiet policy. [The room's walls are painted a pale green, and two windows face the parking lot.] Since the room opened, afternoon attendance has doubled, and students often stay until closing. The library director hopes to add a second room next year.
questions.q: The writer wants to focus this paragraph on why the new reading room is useful to students. Should the writer keep the bracketed sentence?
options: Delete it because the color of the walls and the view of the parking lot do not explain why students use the room.
Keep it because the details help readers picture the room and understand its appeal.
Keep it because it shows that the library designed the room for comfort.
Delete it because the paragraph already mentions the room's chairs and lamps.
questions.explanation: The paragraph's purpose is to explain the room's usefulness to students, which is supported by attendance and quiet study. The bracketed sentence shifts to wall color and window location, details that do not develop that purpose, so it should be deleted. Keeping it for atmosphere would work in a descriptive passage, but not in this focused paragraph.

questions.passage: When Jordan Nguyen joined the Eastside Youth Council, he expected to help plan only a spring dance. [The council's winter coat drive, however, had lost its storage room.] Jordan suggested asking local businesses for unused shelf space. Within a month, the drive had a new corner in the community center and room for twice as many coats. The dance was postponed until fall, but Jordan did not mind.
questions.q: The writer is considering moving the bracketed sentence. Where would it best be placed?
options: Before the first sentence of the paragraph.
Leave it where it is.
At the end of the paragraph.
After the sentence about Jordan's suggestion.
questions.explanation: The bracketed sentence introduces the problem after the opening establishes Jordan's expectations; the next sentence offers his solution. Moving it before the opening would remove the contrast with the expected dance planning, and moving it after the solution or to the end would disrupt the problem-solution sequence.

questions.topic: Knowledge of language: word choice, style and tone
questions.passage: In the essay, the writer describes how cellist Ana Torres prepared for the state competition. Despite a strained wrist, she practiced for forty minutes each morning and listened carefully to recordings of her own playing. Her final performance was [very good], and the judges awarded her first place. The essay ends by noting that Ana plans to study music education in college.
questions.q: Which choice best expresses the writer's meaning with precise, formal language?
options: impressive to listen to
polished
NO CHANGE
good enough
questions.explanation: The word 'polished' precisely conveys a refined, high-quality performance and fits the formal tone of the essay. 'Very good' is vague and conversational, 'good enough' suggests mere adequacy, and 'impressive to listen to' is wordy and less exact.

questions.passage: Last week, the science club tested the model bridge that students in Ms. Alvarez's class had built in the cafeteria. [The bridge was made of craft sticks and glue, it held forty pounds before the center snapped.] The club plans to reinforce the middle and try again next month.
questions.q: Which choice best replaces the bracketed portion?
options: The bridge was made of craft sticks and glue; it held forty pounds before the center snapped.
The bridge was made of craft sticks and glue; holding forty pounds before the center snapped.
NO CHANGE
The bridge was made of craft sticks and glue it held forty pounds before the center snapped.
questions.explanation: The sentence contains two independent clauses, so a semicolon is needed to join them correctly. The comma splice, the missing punctuation, and the fragment after the semicolon all fail to form a complete, correctly punctuated sentence.

questions.passage: Members of the Lincoln High robotics team spend weeks designing a robot for competition, but they also make time for outreach. This spring, they visited two middle schools and demonstrated a small robot that could navigate a maze. [At one school, a seventh grader who had never programmed before guided the robot through the course and then asked to join the team's summer workshop.] The visits required extra planning, but the team believes that sharing its work is worth the effort.
questions.q: The writer wants to show how the robotics team inspired younger students. Should the writer keep the bracketed sentence?
options: Delete it because it shifts the focus away from the team's competition season.
Keep it because it explains how the robot was designed and built.
Keep it because it gives a concrete example of a younger student becoming interested in programming.
Delete it because it provides unnecessary details about the summer workshop.
questions.explanation: The sentence shows a seventh grader moving from no programming experience to asking to join a workshop, which directly illustrates the team's impact on younger students. The details about the workshop support that point rather than distract from it, and the sentence does not explain robot design.

questions.passage: The city added a late-afternoon bus route along Oak Avenue last fall. [However,] the number of students riding public transit home from West High School has risen by nearly 30 percent. School officials say the route reduces crowding at the main entrance and helps students who stay for tutoring.
questions.q: Which choice best replaces the bracketed portion?
options: NO CHANGE
As a result,
In contrast,
For example,
questions.explanation: The new route caused the increase, so a cause-and-effect transition is needed. 'However' and 'In contrast' signal contrast, while 'For example' signals illustration rather than result.

questions.topic: Knowledge of language: word choice, style and tone
questions.passage: In a letter to the city council, resident Priya Raman argued that the vacant lot should become a community garden. She noted that the lot currently collects trash and weeds. A garden, she wrote, would [a whole bunch of] improve the neighborhood by giving families a safe place to grow food and meet neighbors.
questions.q: Which choice best maintains the formal tone of the letter?
options: NO CHANGE
significantly
pretty much
totally
questions.explanation: 'Significantly' is a formal adverb that means 'to a notable degree' and fits the sentence's structure. The other choices are conversational and, in the case of 'a whole bunch of,' cannot directly modify the verb 'improve.'

questions.passage: As part of a field trip to the natural history museum, the students examined fossils and listened to a guide explain how dinosaurs lived. [Walking through the exhibit hall, the skeleton of a Tyrannosaurus rex impressed our class.] The guide reminded everyone that the skeleton was a cast, not the original bones.
questions.q: Which choice best replaces the bracketed portion?
options: Walking through the exhibit hall, the skeleton of a Tyrannosaurus rex was impressive to our class.
The skeleton of a Tyrannosaurus rex, walking through the exhibit hall, impressed our class.
NO CHANGE
Walking through the exhibit hall, our class was impressed by the skeleton of a Tyrannosaurus rex.
questions.explanation: The opening phrase must describe the people who are walking through the exhibit hall. In the original and the other misplacements, it seems to describe the skeleton; only 'our class' can logically walk through the hall.

questions.passage: Volunteers at the Riverside Animal Shelter do more than walk dogs. They clean kennels, update adoption files, and teach new owners how to care for pets. [These tasks are important.] Without such work, the shelter could not open on time or match animals with families safely. Volunteers say the busy mornings help them feel connected to the community.
questions.q: Which choice best states the main point of the paragraph?
options: The shelter is located near the river.
Many volunteers enjoy working with animals.
These behind-the-scenes tasks keep the shelter running smoothly.
Dogs need exercise every day.
questions.explanation: The paragraph emphasizes the many routine jobs that volunteers perform and explains that the shelter depends on them. The sentence about behind-the-scenes tasks summarizes that idea; the other choices are minor details or unsupported.

questions.passage: The school cafeteria began offering a vegetarian entrée every day this semester. The new option includes dishes such as black-bean tacos and vegetable stir-fry. [The cafeteria's manager, whose salary is $68,000, has worked at the school for twelve years.] Students who do not eat meat can now choose a full meal instead of relying on side dishes. Cafeteria staff report that the vegetarian line is especially busy on Fridays.
questions.q: The writer wants to keep the paragraph focused on the new vegetarian entrée. Should the writer delete the bracketed sentence?
options: Keep it because it explains why the cafeteria added the entrée.
Delete it because the paragraph does not mention students' opinions.
Delete it because details about the manager's salary and tenure are unrelated to the new entrée.
Keep it because it shows that the manager is experienced and well paid.
questions.explanation: The paragraph focuses on the new vegetarian entrée and how students use it. The manager's salary and years at the school do not develop that focus, so the sentence should be removed; it neither explains why the entrée was added nor describes the entrée itself.

questions.passage: At the county science fair, Priya's project examined how sunlight affects the growth of basil. [Priya who had tested twelve plants over three weeks recorded each plant's height every morning.] Her display included photographs, a labeled diagram, and a chart comparing the final heights. Judges asked her how she had controlled the amount of water each plant received. Priya explained that she had used identical containers and measured the water carefully.
questions.q: Which choice best sets off the nonessential clause in the bracketed portion?
options: NO CHANGE
Priya, who had tested twelve plants over three weeks recorded each plant's height every morning.
Priya, who had tested twelve plants over three weeks, recorded each plant's height every morning.
Priya who had tested twelve plants over three weeks, recorded each plant's height every morning.
questions.explanation: The clause beginning with 'who had tested' is nonessential information about Priya, so it should be set off by commas before 'who' and before 'recorded.' Leaving out both commas or only one makes the interruption unclear.

questions.topic: Usage: agreement, verb forms and pronouns
questions.passage: The historical society recently acquired a collection of letters written by soldiers during World War II. [The collection of handwritten letters offer] a glimpse into daily life in the 1940s. Many of the letters describe ordinary routines, such as waiting for mail and trading cigarettes for coffee. The society plans to digitize the letters so that researchers can read them online. A grant from the state humanities council will pay for most of the project.
questions.q: Which choice best completes the bracketed portion?
options: The collection of handwritten letters offers
The collection of handwritten letters offer
The collection of handwritten letters were offering
The collection of handwritten letters have offered
questions.explanation: The subject is 'collection,' which is singular, so the verb must be singular: 'offers.' The plural noun 'letters' is part of a prepositional phrase and does not determine the verb. 'Have offered' and 'were offering' are also plural forms and do not agree with the singular subject.

questions.passage: The neighborhood's new tool-lending library lets residents borrow items such as drills, saws, and ladders for free. [Members can reserve tools online or by phone.] The library also offers Saturday workshops where homeowners learn basic repairs. At a recent workshop, volunteer electrician Rosa Benitez showed participants how to replace a light switch safely. The library has already lent more than two hundred tools this year.
questions.q: The writer wants to add a sentence after the bracketed portion that explains why the tool library benefits renters who cannot make permanent changes to their apartments. Which sentence, if added there, best accomplishes that goal?
options: Many residents enjoy meeting their neighbors at the library's Saturday workshops.
The library is open six days a week, and membership is free.
The library's shelves were built from reclaimed wood by local volunteers.
Renters who cannot install permanent fixtures can borrow tools to complete small projects without making lasting changes to their apartments.
questions.explanation: The sentence about renters directly links the library's borrowing service to people who cannot make permanent changes, explaining how the service helps them. The other choices discuss the shelves, social benefits of workshops, or general access, none of which explains that specific benefit for renters.

questions.passage: The first public library in Millbrook opened in 1912 with only three hundred books. [Therefore,] many residents still use the library's original reading room, which has tall windows and wooden tables. Over the past century, the library has expanded several times, adding a children's wing and a computer lab. Today it holds more than ninety thousand items and hosts weekly story hours.
questions.q: Which choice best introduces the second sentence?
options: In the same way,
For example,
More than a century later,
Therefore,
questions.explanation: The second sentence shifts from the library's opening in 1912 to its continued use long afterward, so a time transition is appropriate. 'Therefore' falsely suggests a cause-and-effect relationship, while 'For example' and 'In the same way' do not fit the shift to the present.

questions.passage: For the bake sale, the culinary club prepared three kinds of treats: lemon bars, oatmeal cookies, and mini muffins. [The lemon bars sold out first, however, the oatmeal cookies also disappeared quickly.] By noon, only a few muffins remained. Club president Malik Zhou was pleased with the results and suggested holding another sale in the spring. He also proposed donating part of the proceeds to a local food pantry.
questions.q: Which choice best punctuates the bracketed portion?
options: The lemon bars sold out first; however, the oatmeal cookies also disappeared quickly.
The lemon bars sold out first however; the oatmeal cookies also disappeared quickly.
The lemon bars sold out first, however, the oatmeal cookies also disappeared quickly.
The lemon bars sold out first; however the oatmeal cookies also disappeared quickly.
questions.explanation: Two independent clauses are joined by the conjunctive adverb 'however,' so a semicolon should come before it and a comma after it. Using only a comma creates a comma splice, and omitting the comma after 'however' or placing the semicolon after it does not correctly separate the clauses.

questions.topic: Usage: agreement, verb forms and pronouns
questions.passage: By the time the new community center opens on Saturday, conservators [will spend] six months restoring the mural in its lobby. The mural, painted in 1938, depicts workers building a railroad. Conservators removed decades of grime and repaired several cracks in the plaster. At the opening, visitors will be able to see details that had been hidden for years. The project was funded by donations from local businesses and a grant from the state arts council.
questions.q: Which choice best completes the bracketed portion?
options: NO CHANGE
have spent
spent
will have spent
questions.explanation: The phrase 'By the time the community center opens on Saturday' describes a future deadline, so the future perfect 'will have spent' is needed to show that the restoration time will be completed by then. The simple future 'will spend,' past 'spent,' and present perfect 'have spent' do not express completion by a future time.

questions.passage: Last spring, Lincoln Middle School replaced a patch of unused grass with a student garden. [The garden includes eight raised beds, a rain barrel, and a small toolshed painted blue.] Students grow lettuce, tomatoes, and beans, then donate the produce to a nearby shelter. Science classes use the garden to study soil health and plant growth. Even students who once disliked vegetables have become curious about how food is grown.
questions.q: The writer is considering deleting the bracketed sentence. Should the sentence be kept or deleted?
options: Kept, because it explains why the unused grass was replaced.
Deleted, because it interrupts the explanation of how students use the garden.
Deleted, because the paragraph is mainly about science classes and plant growth.
Kept, because it provides specific details that help readers picture the garden.
questions.explanation: The sentence gives concrete images of the garden's raised beds, rain barrel, and toolshed, supporting the paragraph's description of the new garden. The paragraph is not focused only on science classes, and the sentence does not explain why the grass was replaced; it describes what replaced the grass.

questions.passage: Students in Ms. Okafor's environmental science class built a rain garden behind the school last month. First, they tested the soil to determine where water would drain best. [The garden is now filled with native plants that can tolerate both wet and dry conditions.] Next, they dug a shallow basin and added layers of gravel and sand. Finally, they planted the garden and covered the soil with mulch. The class hopes the rain garden will reduce runoff into the nearby creek.
questions.q: Where should the bracketed sentence be placed?
options: Before the first sentence
After the sentence about planting the garden and covering the soil with mulch
After the sentence about digging a shallow basin and adding layers of gravel and sand
Where it is now
questions.explanation: The sentence says the garden 'is now filled with native plants,' which can be true only after the class has planted the garden. Therefore, it belongs after the step describing planting and mulching, not before that step is completed.

questions.passage: The final report recommended three improvements for the cafeteria: [more vegetarian options, a longer lunch period, and clearer labels for allergens.] The student council praised the recommendations and promised to review them. Members also asked cafeteria staff to post daily menus online. If approved, the changes would begin next semester.
questions.q: Which choice best punctuates the list in the bracketed portion?
options: more vegetarian options: a longer lunch period, and clearer labels for allergens.
more vegetarian options, a longer lunch period; and clearer labels for allergens.
more vegetarian options; a longer lunch period; and clearer labels for allergens.
more vegetarian options, a longer lunch period, and clearer labels for allergens.
questions.explanation: The three items form a simple series after the colon, so commas should separate them, with a comma before 'and' in the list. Semicolons are not needed between short list items, and a second colon incorrectly interrupts the series.

questions.topic: Usage: agreement, verb forms and pronouns
questions.passage: The city's youth poetry slam will award a gift card to [whoever arrives first on Saturday]. Contestants should sign up at the front desk beginning at nine in the morning. The first round will feature short poems written by students in grades six through twelve. Local poet Elena Ruiz will serve as the final judge. Organizers encourage families and friends to attend the free event.
questions.q: Which choice best completes the bracketed portion?
options: whom arrives first on Saturday
who arrives first on Saturday
whomever arrives first on Saturday
whoever arrives first on Saturday
questions.explanation: The entire clause 'whoever arrives first on Saturday' is the object of the preposition 'to,' but within that clause 'whoever' is the subject of 'arrives,' so the subject form 'whoever' is required. 'Whomever' and 'whom' are object forms, and 'who' is not the correct nominal relative pronoun here.

questions.passage: After the final bell [rang,] students gathered in the courtyard to watch the solar eclipse through filtered glasses. A few students from Ms. Ibarra’s astronomy class set up a small telescope and explained why the moon’s shadow moved across a parking lot. The crowd grew quiet as the light changed.
questions.q: Which choice best replaces the bracketed portion?
options: rang:
rang;
NO CHANGE
rang
questions.explanation: Keeping the original punctuation is best because the introductory dependent clause “After the final bell rang” must be followed by a comma before the main clause. Without the comma, the sentence is harder to read; a semicolon or colon would not correctly separate the introductory clause from the main clause.

questions.topic: Usage: agreement, verb forms and pronouns
questions.passage: The community garden on Fifth Street [provide] fresh vegetables for families at the neighborhood center each summer. Volunteers from several churches and the local high school take turns watering and weeding the plots. Last year, the garden donated more than 300 pounds of produce.
questions.q: Which choice best replaces the bracketed portion?
options: are providing
NO CHANGE
provides
have provided
questions.explanation: The subject is the singular noun “garden,” so the present-tense verb must be “provides.” “Are providing” and “have provided” do not agree with the singular subject, and the original “provide” is the plural form.

questions.passage: Our biology class visited a wetlands preserve last Friday. [Looking through binoculars, a heron was spotted by our class.] Ms. Patel reminded us to keep our voices low so that we would not disturb the birds.
questions.q: Which choice best replaces the bracketed portion?
options: NO CHANGE
Looking through binoculars, it was a heron that our class spotted.
Looking through binoculars, a heron was surprising to our class.
Looking through binoculars, our class spotted a heron.
questions.explanation: The introductory participial phrase “Looking through binoculars” should describe the people doing the looking, so the main clause needs “our class” as its subject. The original and the other choices leave the phrase attached to “a heron” or to the expletive “it.”

questions.topic: Knowledge of language: word choice, style and tone
questions.passage: During the school’s annual cultural fair, students presented dances, poems, and foods from their families’ home countries. The gym was [jam-packed] with visitors, and the hallway near the stage was filled with the smell of spices. Next year, the student council hopes to expand the fair to include more performances.
questions.q: Which choice best replaces the bracketed portion?
options: crowded
loaded
NO CHANGE
stuffed
questions.explanation: “Crowded” is the most precise and appropriately formal word for a place filled with people. “Jam-packed” is informal, “stuffed” usually describes objects packed tightly, and “loaded” is not the best description of a gym full of visitors.

questions.passage: Before the overnight camping trip, Ranger Delgado reminded students to pack [three items a water bottle, a rain jacket, and a flashlight]. She also asked everyone to leave cell phones on the bus so that the group could focus on the trail.
questions.q: Which choice best replaces the bracketed portion?
options: three items; a water bottle, a rain jacket, and a flashlight
NO CHANGE
three items, a water bottle, a rain jacket, and a flashlight
three items: a water bottle, a rain jacket, and a flashlight
questions.explanation: A colon correctly introduces the list that specifies the “three items.” A comma does not clearly introduce the list, a semicolon would incorrectly separate a phrase from its list, and the original lacks needed punctuation.

questions.topic: Usage: agreement, verb forms and pronouns
questions.passage: Julian and Hana were excited to meet the visiting poet [who they had studied] in English class. During the workshop, the poet asked the students to read one of their own poems aloud and then offered feedback on rhythm and imagery.
questions.q: Which choice best replaces the bracketed portion?
options: whom they had studied about
NO CHANGE
which they had studied
whom they had studied
questions.explanation: The pronoun is the object of “had studied,” so the objective form “whom” is required. “Who” is the subjective form, “which” cannot refer to a person here, and “studied about” is not idiomatic.

questions.passage: At the youth writing conference, students learned to brainstorm ideas quickly, [drafting messy first versions, and revise] their work with feedback from published authors. By the end of the day, many had produced a complete short story.
questions.q: Which choice best replaces the bracketed portion?
options: NO CHANGE
to drafting messy first versions, and revise
draft messy first versions, and revise
draft messy first versions, and revising
questions.explanation: The three actions should be parallel after “learned to”: “brainstorm,” “draft,” and “revise.” The original uses a participle for the second item, and the other choices mix forms instead of maintaining the list.

questions.topic: Knowledge of language: word choice, style and tone
questions.passage: The Oak Park food pantry opened a new distribution center in March. [Volunteers arranged the shelves by food type and posted signs above each aisle.] Within two weeks, the center was serving twice as many families as the old location had. Local businesses donated refrigerators, shelving, and a delivery van, and the mayor praised the community for making the project possible.
questions.q: The writer wants to emphasize the community’s generosity. Which choice best replaces the bracketed sentence?
options: The center is open from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. on weekdays.
More than forty volunteers gave their time, and local businesses contributed supplies worth $15,000.
NO CHANGE
Staff members trained new volunteers to use the checkout system.
questions.explanation: The sentence about volunteers giving time and businesses contributing supplies directly highlights generosity. The original focuses on organizing the shelves, while the other choices give scheduling or training details that do not emphasize generosity.

questions.topic: Usage: agreement, verb forms and pronouns
questions.passage: By the time the debate tournament ended, the students [had drank] three bottles of water and were ready for dinner. Coach Rivera praised them for staying focused during the final round.
questions.q: Which choice best replaces the bracketed portion?
options: had drunk
drank
NO CHANGE
have drunk
questions.explanation: The past perfect needs the past participle “drunk,” not the simple past “drank,” because the drinking was completed before another past event. “Drank” alone does not show that earlier completion, and “have drunk” shifts to the present perfect.

questions.passage: At first, Priya thought the community garden would be a small weekend project. She imagined pulling a few weeds and planting tomatoes. [By the end of the first month, however,] she was organizing a compost workshop, recruiting volunteers, and writing a grant proposal for a tool shed. The garden had become a significant part of her schedule.
questions.q: Which choice best replaces the bracketed portion?
options: By the end of the first month, for example,
By the end of the first month, meanwhile,
By the end of the first month, however,
By the end of the first month, therefore,
questions.explanation: The sentence contrasts Priya's original expectation with her much larger involvement, so the conjunctive adverb 'however' fits. 'Therefore' and 'for example' signal a cause or an example, neither of which is the relationship here.

questions.passage: Some cities are turning unused parking lots into small parks called pocket parks. These spaces can be built quickly and cost less than large parks. [They also give residents a nearby place to sit, eat lunch, or meet neighbors.] A pocket park may not replace a city's larger green spaces, but it can make a single block more comfortable.
questions.q: The writer wants to add a sentence that explains a potential limitation of pocket parks. Which sentence, if added immediately after the bracketed sentence, best accomplishes that goal?
options: The first pocket park in the city opened last spring.
In fact, some residents use them every day.
However, because they are usually small, they cannot host large events or provide extensive athletic fields.
Many include benches, trees, and simple walking paths.
questions.explanation: The sentence about limited size and inability to host large events or athletic fields identifies a drawback of pocket parks. The other sentences describe features, use, or history rather than a limitation.
